intro/hello: This is chapter eleven: self-supervised learning and CLIP.
intro/labels: Every classifier in the first course learned from labels: a million photos, each tagged by a person.
intro/thin: Labels are expensive, and thin: one word per image says nothing about pose, texture or light.
intro/before: CS231n ended with autoencoders and GANs, which learn from images alone by rebuilding pixels. Their features never matched supervised ones.
intro/changed: Between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-one, that changed: networks trained on unlabeled images matched supervised pretraining, then beat it.
intro/clip: And clip learned from four hundred million captioned images, and could classify things it was never trained to classify.
intro/plan: We will build the central idea, the contrastive loss, and see why it needs negatives.
intro/plan2: Then sim C L R, moe co and clip, and finally the two other families: masked autoencoders, and dee no.
intro/grade: But first: with no labels, how do we know the features are any good?
probe/self: Self-supervised learning means inventing a task whose answers come from the data itself.
probe/lm: Language models already do this: predicting the next word turns any sentence into training data.
probe/rot: For images, the early tasks were puzzles. Rotate a photo by a quarter turn, a half, or three quarters, and ask the network which.
probe/why: To tell which way is up, it has to know something about skies, legs and wheels.
probe/point: The puzzle itself never matters. We want an encoder, f, whose features are useful later.
probe/probe: So we grade them with a linear probe: freeze the encoder, and train only a linear classifier on top, with labels.
probe/meaning: If a single matrix multiply can read the class off the features, the encoder has made the class explicit.
probe/acc: Its test accuracy is the grade. When a paper reports seventy six point five percent on ImageNet, it usually means this.
views/idea: Here is the idea that won. Make two random versions of an image: two views. They differ pixel by pixel, but show the same thing.
views/crop: Crop a different region for each, maybe flip one,
views/color: then shift the colors, or drop them to gray.
views/rule: Now train the encoder so that two views of one image land close together, and views of different images far apart.
views/nolabel: Nobody says what a cat is. To match views across crops and color shifts, the network must describe each image by what stays the same: its content.
views/teacher: So the augmentations are the real teacher. Without color jitter, two crops share their colors, and the network cheats by matching color.
views/norm: To measure close, each embedding, z, is first scaled to length one.
views/cos: Then the dot product of two embeddings is the cosine of their angle: one when they point the same way, minus one when opposite.
views/sphere: Every embedding lives on a sphere, and similarity is just an angle.
infonce/table: Take a batch of N images. Put view one of each image down the rows, and view two across the columns.
infonce/S: Each cell is a similarity, divided by a temperature, tau. Call this table S.
infonce/right: In row i, exactly one column is right: column i, the other view of the same image. The other N minus one are wrong.
infonce/softmax: That is classification with N classes. A softmax along each row turns scores into probabilities.
infonce/ce: Then take minus the log of the probability on the diagonal, and average over the rows.
infonce/name: This is info N C E, named in twenty eighteen by van den Oord and colleagues.
infonce/weights: Row i is a softmax classifier whose class weights are the other view's embeddings. Every image is its own class.
infonce/pull: The top of the fraction pulls the partner closer. The bottom pushes every other image away.
infonce/logN: If every embedding were the same, every row would be a uniform guess, and the loss would be exactly log N.
temperature/narrow: Why divide by tau? Cosines only range from minus one to one, which is too narrow for a confident softmax.
temperature/small: With tau at zero point one, a gap of one in cosine becomes a gap of ten in the score.
temperature/grad: tau also decides which negatives matter. The gradient of one row's loss is simple: the probabilities, minus the one-hot target.
temperature/push: So each negative is pushed away in proportion to its probability: how much the row confuses it with the partner.
temperature/large: With a large tau, the probabilities are flat, and every negative gets about the same push.
temperature/lower: Lower tau, and the softmax sharpens. Nearly all of the push goes to the few closest negatives: the hard negatives.
temperature/values: In practice tau is small: moe co used zero point zero seven, and clip starts there and learns it.
collapse/why: Why not drop the bottom of the fraction, and just pull matching views together?
collapse/trivial: Because a perfect answer learns nothing: map every image to the same point. Every pair matches, and the loss is as low as it goes.
collapse/name: That is collapse, and every self-supervised method has to prevent it somehow.
collapse/toy: Here is a toy. Each item has two numbers of content and four of style. A view keeps the content and redraws the style.
collapse/init: The circle shows each item's embedding, colored by a hidden class. At first the classes are mixed, and a linear probe gets about half right.
collapse/train: Train with info N C E. The classes gather into arcs, the batch matrix lights up along its diagonal, and the probe passes ninety percent.
collapse/forces: Two forces are at work: alignment pulls matching views together, and uniformity spreads everything around the circle.
collapse/pos: Now train with positives only. At first it learns to ignore style, and looks fine.
collapse/fall: Then nothing stops the drift. Every point slides to one spot, the matrix goes flat, and the probe falls toward chance. The loss never complained.
simclr/who: sim C L R, from Chen and colleagues in twenty twenty, put these pieces together in the simplest form.
simclr/views: Every image in a batch of N gets two views, so there are two N views in all.
simclr/f: A ResNet encoder, f, turns each view into a representation, h, of two thousand and forty eight numbers.
simclr/g: A small projection head, g, maps h to the one hundred and twenty eight numbers, z, that the loss sees.
simclr/S: Every view is compared with every other. Its similarity with itself is removed, and its partner is the one right answer among two N minus one.
simclr/keep: After training, the head is thrown away and h is kept: it beat z by more than ten points.
simclr/aug: The mix of augmentations mattered most: random crops, plus strong color distortion.
simclr/batch: And it wants big batches: four thousand and ninety six images, so eight thousand one hundred and ninety negatives for every positive pair.
simclr/result: A linear probe on a ResNet fifty, four times as wide, reached seventy six point five percent on ImageNet, as good as a supervised ResNet fifty.
moco/cost: Batches of four thousand need a lot of hardware. moe co, from He and colleagues in twenty nineteen, found negatives elsewhere.
moco/queue: It keeps a queue of embeddings from recent batches. Every step, new keys go in, and the oldest come out.
moco/many: So each query meets sixty five thousand negatives, while the batch stays at two hundred and fifty six.
moco/catch: The catch is consistency: an old key was made by an older encoder, so old keys and new queries use different rulers.
moco/two: So moe co uses two encoders. The query encoder, f q, is trained by backprop.
moco/ema: The key encoder, f k, gets no gradient at all. After every step, it moves a small fraction of the way toward f q.
moco/avg: That is a moving average with momentum m. At zero point nine nine nine, the key encoder remembers roughly the last thousand steps.
moco/smooth: It follows the query encoder smoothly, with a lag, so every key in the queue comes from nearly the same network.
moco/fail: Copying the encoder outright, m at zero, made training fail. And the momentum encoder outlived the queue: dee no still uses one.
clip/pairs: Contrastive learning needs pairs that should match. clip, from OpenAI in twenty twenty-one, used pairs the internet already had: an image, and the text next to it.
clip/data: Its training set was four hundred million image and text pairs.
clip/towers: There are two encoders: for images, a ResNet or a vision transformer; for text, a transformer.
clip/shared: Both project into the same space, normalized, so an image and a sentence can be compared with a dot product.
clip/matrix: In a batch of N pairs, image i should pick caption i out of all N captions,
clip/sym: and caption i should pick image i out of all N images. That is info N C E in both directions: along the rows, and down the columns.
clip/toy: Here is a toy clip: pictures of colored shapes, with captions like, a big red circle. Watch the diagonal sharpen.
clip/order: Color is learned first. Telling a circle from a square takes longest, and those cells are the last to fade.
clip/tau: The temperature is learned, starting at zero point zero seven. And the real batch held thirty two thousand pairs.
clip/why: Predicting each caption word for word was tried first. Matching was several times more efficient, and it is exactly what classification needs.
zeroshot/free: Once images and text share a space, a classifier needs no training at all.
zeroshot/prompts: Write one sentence per class. In the toy: a circle, a square, a triangle. For real photos: a photo of a dog, a photo of a cat.
zeroshot/embed: Embed the sentences with the text encoder. Those vectors are the weights of the classifier.
zeroshot/image: Then embed each image, compare it with every sentence, and pick the most similar.
zeroshot/linear: It is a linear classifier, like those of the first course, except that you wrote its weights in English.
zeroshot/zero: This is zero-shot: zero training examples of these classes. Any list of classes you can name will do.
zeroshot/result: clip's best model classified ImageNet this way at seventy six point two percent, matching a supervised ResNet fifty without any of its labeled images.
zeroshot/wording: The wording matters. The template, a photo of a label, beat the bare class name by one point three points, and averaging eighty templates added three point five more.
zeroshot/uses: clip's embeddings became infrastructure: Stable Diffusion listens to its text encoder, and many vision-language models see through its image encoder.
mae/back: The second family goes back to the autoencoder, and borrows a trick from BERT: hide part of the input, then rebuild it.
mae/mae: M A E, from He and colleagues in twenty twenty-one, cuts an image into patches and hides a random seventy five percent of them.
mae/enc: The encoder, a vit, sees only the visible quarter: no placeholders, just those patches and their positions.
mae/dec: A small decoder adds a learned mask token in every gap, and predicts the missing pixels.
mae/loss: The loss is the squared error on the hidden patches only. Copying the visible ones would be trivial.
mae/why: Why so much? BERT hides fifteen percent of words, but images are redundant: a hidden patch usually looks like its neighbors.
mae/naive: Here the holes are filled with no learning at all, by averaging nearby pixels. With a quarter hidden, that works well.
mae/hard: At seventy five percent, it smears every edge. To do better, a network has to know what birds and wheels look like.
mae/cheap: A bonus: the big encoder sees only a quarter of the tokens, so training ran about three times faster.
mae/result: M A E features are weaker under a linear probe, but excellent after fine-tuning: a vit Huge reached eighty seven point eight percent on ImageNet.
dino/third: The third family has no negatives and no pixels. dee no, from Caron and colleagues in twenty twenty-one, trains a student to match a teacher.
dino/teacher: The teacher is the same network, with weights that are a moving average of the student's, as in moe co. Nobody provides the right answer.
dino/outputs: Both end in a softmax over many outputs, soft clusters it invents. The student matches the teacher's distribution on another view.
dino/crops: The teacher sees large crops; the student also sees small ones, so it must recognize the whole from a part.
dino/collapse: With no negatives, what stops collapse? Two cheap operations on the teacher's output.
dino/center: Centering subtracts a running average of the outputs, so no single output can win for every image.
dino/sharpen: Sharpening gives the teacher a lower temperature than the student, so its targets are always more decisive.
dino/nocenter: On the toy data: drop centering, and one output swallows everything.
dino/nosharpen: Drop sharpening instead, and every output flattens toward uniform.
dino/both: Together, they balance: outputs that split along the hidden groups, without ever seeing a label.
dino/emerge: Its vision transformers also learned attention that outlines the main object, with no segmentation labels. A vit Base reached eighty point one percent with a linear probe.
outro/con: Contrastive learning matches two views against a batch of negatives: sim C L R gets them from huge batches, moe co from a queue.
outro/clip: clip applies the same loss to images and captions, and its shared space turns prompts into classifiers.
outro/mae: M A E hides three quarters of an image and rebuilds the pixels.
outro/dino: dee no matches a moving-average teacher, kept alive by centering and sharpening.
outro/probe: And all of them are graded the same way: freeze the encoder, and see what a linear probe can read.
outro/flavors: Contrastive and dee no features are ready for probes and nearest neighbors; M A E features want fine-tuning, and improve with size.
outro/thread: The common thread: the data supplies its own targets. Two views of a photo, a caption, a hidden patch, or a slower copy of the network itself.
outro/close: Labels are still needed, but only a few, at the very end, to read the answer off features that were learned without them.
